newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - U.S. rate worries dominate, Eurobourses fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. rate worries dominate, Eurobourses fall.

text.p: British, German and French stocks fell sharply in morning business on Monday amid cautious trade ahead of an important U.S. interest rate meeting on Tuesday.
On the currency markets, the dollar was steady, with trading volumes low in the absence of the Tokyo market, which was closed for a holiday.
However, the mark lost ground against European currencies, particularly the French franc, following the weekend European finance ministers' meeting in Dublin.
The gathering pace of Europe's drive towards monetary union, not only put pressure on mark but also lifted the European currency unit to 21-month high.
On Friday the mark slipped to a two-month low against the franc. It weakened further to a 3-1/2 month low early on Monday to around 3.3810 francs before recovering slightly.
But, as with the stock markets, the rate-setting meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Markets Committee overshadowed currency trading:

"Having ridden on the crest of a wave of optimism about EMU prospects, foreign exchange markets will shift their attention back to monetary policy this week, with the key event clearly being the FOMC meeting on Tuesday," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

A Reuter survey last week showed that 17 of 30 economists polled thought the FOMC meeting would raise rates, but few in the market were talking about an increase bigger than one quarter of a percentage point.
Leading London stocks had slumped about one percent, or 40 points, in value by 1030 GMT. Declining shares were in an eight-to-one majority and volume was a modest 125 million shares.
Traders said the market was unlikely to make any major move before a regular British rate-setting monetary meeting on Monday and Tuesday's FOMC were out of the way.
"People will just be sitting tight, desperately keen to keep out of trouble," said one trader.

Any pressure for a rate increase from Bank of England Governor Eddie George at the British policy discussion was likely to be rebuffed by Chancellor (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke, analysts said. A Reuters poll of 20 economists found a unanimous prediction of no change in rates.
On Friday, the blue chip FTSE 100 index closed down 10 points after hitting an intraday peak of 3,994.1 -- just short of the psychologically-important 4,000 level.
In Frankfurt, the DAX index opened lower and proceeded to deepen its losses to 0.75 percent by 1030 GMT. Dealers said buying was on hold ahead of a U.S. rates decision.

And on the Paris bourse, shares also started lower and dropped further on profit-taking with dealers cautious about U.S. rates and because of book squaring on the last day of the September accounting period.
Dealers said the firming of the franc against the mark was not helping shares.
On the precious metals market, platinum fixed at the lowest level for nearly 2-1/2 years as weakness in silver pressured the rest of the precious metals complex.
Platinum fixed at $386.50 per ounce, the lowest since April 20, 1994, compared with $387.25 on Friday afternoon.
Heavy selling by US investment funds and other speculators last week shaved 13 cents off the price of spot silver, pushing it below the key $5.00 per ounce level.
In addition, major platinum producer Russia was rumoured to be stepping up selling to earn hard cash to plug holes in its budget.
CURRENCIES AT 1030 GMT
The dollar was at 1.5155 marks and 109.85 yen compared with 1.5141 marks and 109.76 yen in Europe late on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1030 GMT
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares had fallen 40.8 points to 3,923.3.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index dropped 14.96 to 2,063.50.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was down 19.33 at 2,626.77. PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $381.20 compared with a close at $381.75 in London on Friday. Silver was $4.88.
